content:
Build a vacuum system out of a parts library (chambers, tubes, fittings, valves, pumps, gauges, leaks), then watch it pump down from atmosphere to UHV. The gas dynamics are regime-aware, and everything runs client-side in the browser.
Code: github.com/sinkomr/ConductVac
What it does A live pressure colormap over the schematic, spanning 12 decades, including the gradients along the plumbing. Gauges that lie realistically: gas-species sensitivity, response lag, noise, Pirani flatline, cold-cathode strike failures, hot-cathode filament trips, and the X-ray limit. The strip charts overlay the true pressure so you can watch your gauges deceive you. A gas-load flow view from sources (leaks, outgassing, permeation) through the network to the pumps, which answers “what limits my base pressure?” Multiple gas species, bakeout, gas ballast, helium spray on leaks, LN₂ cold traps, and chamber payloads whose surface area drives outgassing. Timeline scripting, plus live interaction: double-click a valve mid-rough-down to see why crossover discipline matters. A catalog of about 80 named commercial pumps and 17 named gauges with nominal datasheet values. Check current manufacturer data before any real design work.
summary: A vacuum system builder and pump-down simulator that runs in the browser.
title: ConductVac

content:
Pack P congruent regular polygons or circles into the smallest regular polygon or circle, and compete for records.
Site: polypack.fly.dev · Code: github.com/sinkomr/PolyPack
What it does The board: drag and rotate pieces that can never overlap. The smallest enclosing container and its size are computed live. Records: published values with their sources, and one live leader per problem. Problems with a proven optimum are closed to entries. Automated search: seven optimizers, seed generators and a contact polish, running in the browser or as a TypeScript library. An API: everything is scriptable, including submitting a packing your own optimizer found. Volunteer computing: a single-file program that searches in the background on spare cores and submits records under your name. More dimensions: beyond the classic flat problems there are curved spaces, polyhedral surfaces, spheres and tori, solids packed in solids, and unit balls on the boundary of 4D polytopes. Problems are written (N, M, P): P pieces with N sides in a container with M sides, with 0 meaning a circle.
summary: Pack congruent polygons or circles into the smallest container, and compete for records.
title: PolyPack

content:
inferplot draws a statistical plot, runs the test that fits the design, and writes the full result on the figure: statistic, degrees of freedom, exact p-value, effect size with its confidence interval, Bayes factor, n and adjusted pairwise comparisons.
It is the Python counterpart of R’s ggstatsplot, tested against its output, and written for AI coding agents and the researchers who check their work.
Code: github.com/sinkomr/inferplot
What it does Five functions, one per question: do independent groups differ (betweenstats), do repeated measurements differ (withinstats), does one sample differ from a value (histostats), are two measurements related (scatterstats), and do the shares of categories differ (barstats). Parametric, nonparametric, robust and Bayesian versions of each test. The result is readable as text and JSON, not just from the image, so an agent (or a person) can check the numbers instead of squinting at a plot. Nothing is ignored silently: unknown arguments raise an error, and arguments that have no effect on the data leave a note. Status: version 0.1, not on PyPI yet. Install it from the repository.
summary: A Python library that draws a statistical plot and writes the full test result on the figure.
title: inferplot

content:
An open method for reviewing a scientific paper claim by claim, with a skill that runs it in Claude and Codex, a prompt that runs it in any other LLM, and a place to post the results.
Code: github.com/sinkomr/OpenPaperReviewer
What a review contains A registry of the paper’s claims, each quoted verbatim with its location. For each claim: what in the paper supports it, whether the cited literature agrees, which ordinary explanations were not excluded, and a verdict from a fixed rubric. A close reading of the references the argument leans on, checking that they say what they are cited for. A verification log of every source the review cites, and a record of the model, effort and prompt that produced it. The result can be audited one claim at a time, and compared with someone else’s review of the same paper.
Limits A review made this way is an AI-assisted draft for a qualified person to check. It is not peer review. The method reviews papers, not people.
summary: An open method for reviewing a scientific paper claim by claim with an LLM.
title: OpenPaperReviewer

content:
HumanBench is a free, browser-based battery of short cognitive tasks. Instead of a single score, it draws your results as a “jagged blob”: one spike per ability, with its uncertainty shown.
Code: github.com/sinkomr/humanbench
It is for curiosity and self-reflection. It is not an IQ test, a clinical assessment, or a basis for decisions about education, employment, or health.
Status: a work in progress.
summary: A free, browser-based battery of short cognitive tasks that draws your results as a jagged blob.
title: HumanBench

content:
A browser tribute to Tetrisphere (H2O Entertainment / Nintendo, N64, 1997), rebuilt from scratch in plain JavaScript with no dependencies, no build step, and original art and music. It plays with a keyboard, a gamepad, or touch.
Code: github.com/sinkomr/spherescue
This is a ground-up reimplementation of the game’s mechanics, not an emulator: no ROM, no ripped assets.
How it works The “sphere” is a lie the original told too. The playfield is a 32×32 grid that wraps in both directions (a torus), drawn with a fisheye projection so it reads as a planet you can scroll around forever.
Modes Free Fable: a 22-level campaign that frees an animated character for every Claude model. Rescue: the classic campaign, ten episodes of ten levels. Puzzle: 100 levels, every one verified solvable within its exact budget of drags and drops. Time Trial: five minutes, maximum score.
summary: A browser tribute to Tetrisphere, rebuilt from scratch in plain JavaScript.
title: Spherescue: Free Fable

content:
I’m Michael Sinko, a physicist in the Bay Area. These days I work on high energy density physics and pulsed power systems at Fisica ATI, and I consult on quantum computing hardware through my company, SQUID Consultants LLC. This site is where I put my public research, projects, and interesting measurements.
So far in this experiment we call life: I grew up in western Pennsylvania, splitting my time between the woods and whatever book I was reading that week (not always mutually exclusive; books only add a few pounds to your camping gear, just make sure the library books stay dry). Scouting kept me busy, I didn’t burn or cut myself (too much), and I earned my Eagle before heading off to college.
I studied physics at Miami University, earning a BS and MS. My first year I set up a PCB prototyping line, and I spent the years after characterizing magnetic materials, mostly nanoparticles and thin films. This was when I first got to play around with cryogenic liquids and high magnetic fields. Much fun! I also discovered intramural broomball and learned to play ice hockey.
My PhD is from Carnegie Mellon, where I worked on 2D materials and superconducting circuits. Most of that happened in cleanrooms and nanofab facilities, so I spent a good chunk of my twenties in a bunny suit. I was also the grill master for our department’s summer cookouts! My two cats, Pico and Nano, kept me company throughout grad school, and I learned to ski in the Appalachians each winter (sans felines).
A postdoc at Sandia National Laboratories brought me west to Livermore, where I set up a nanoimprint lithography system and played with a fancy but frustrating UHV setup. I stayed in the Bay Area afterward, first doing quantum device fabrication at Bleximo, then joining Fisica ATI when Bleximo ceased operations.
When I’m not doing physics, I’m usually woodworking, 3D printing, or out in the garden (which are all still basically physics, right?).
title: About
